title: Severe pre-eclampsia and eclampsia
blurb: Recognise severe pre-eclampsia, give and monitor magnesium sulfate safely, control blood pressure and restrict fluids under NICE NG133.
question: Grace, 34 weeks pregnant with pre-eclampsia, has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure on the antenatal ward. After calling for help, which medicine is the treatment of choice, and how is it given?

teach.body: Formally (NICE NG133): eclampsia is a convulsive condition associated with pre-eclampsia. Severe hypertension means a systolic blood pressure over 160 mmHg or a diastolic over 110 mmHg. In plain English: a woman with pre-eclampsia whose disease is getting worse can fit, and the fit itself is the emergency. The midwife's job is to spot the warning signs early, call for help, and make sure magnesium sulfate, blood pressure control and careful fluids are started and monitored.

What to tell her
rows: Severe pain just below the ribs
Sudden swelling of face, hands or feet
teach.caption: NG133 1.1.1: advise pregnant women to see a healthcare professional immediately with any symptom of pre-eclampsia.

teach.h: Magnesium sulfate: the Collaborative Eclampsia Trial regimen

steps.label: After a fit
steps.sub: Continue for 24 hours after the last fit

steps.label: Recurrent fit
steps.sub: Further 2 to 4 g IV over 5 to 15 minutes

teach.caption: NG133 1.8.4-1.8.5. Do not use diazepam, phenytoin or other anticonvulsants as an alternative to magnesium sulfate in eclampsia.

teach.h: When to consider magnesium before a fit
teach.body: Give magnesium sulfate to a woman in a critical care setting who has, or has previously had, an eclamptic fit. Consider it in severe pre-eclampsia if birth is planned within 24 hours, or if she has severe features: severe headache, problems with vision (blurring, flashing, scotomata), severe pain below the ribs or epigastric pain, nausea or vomiting, oliguria with severe hypertension, or worsening blood results. These are the signs that the brain, liver and kidneys are under strain.

teach.h: Scenario: Grace on the antenatal ward
items: Grace, 34 weeks, had BP 168/112 and a severe headache an hour ago. The midwife now finds her fitting.
The midwife pulls the emergency bell, stays with Grace, keeps her safe and protects her airway with help from the team.
The obstetric team gives magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 5 to 15 minutes, then 1 g per hour, continued for 24 hours after the last fit.
The midwife records reflexes, respiratory rate, BP and hourly urine output, and keeps calcium gluconate to hand.
Maintenance fluids are limited to 80 mL per hour. For the third stage she will receive oxytocin, not oxytocin with ergometrine.

teach.text: Ergometrine (including Syntometrine, oxytocin plus ergometrine) is contraindicated in severe hypertension, pre-eclampsia and eclampsia (NG235 1.10.9). And diazepam or phenytoin are not alternatives to magnesium sulfate for eclamptic fits (NG133 1.8.5).

items: Eclampsia is a convulsive condition associated with pre-eclampsia; severe hypertension is over 160 systolic or over 110 diastolic.
Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 5-15 min, then 1 g/hour for 24 hours (24 hours after the last fit).
Toxicity: lost patellar reflex first, then respiratory depression; calcium gluconate is the antidote.
Labetalol, oral nifedipine or IV hydralazine for severe BP; maintenance fluids limited to 80 mL/hour.
No ergometrine for the third stage in pre-eclampsia or eclampsia.

summary: You can now recognise the warning signs of severe pre-eclampsia, describe the magnesium sulfate regimen for eclampsia and how to monitor for toxicity. You can also explain blood pressure control, the 80 mL per hour limit on maintenance fluids and why ergometrine is avoided.

A.q: A woman with pre-eclampsia at 36 weeks has an eclamptic fit on the labour ward. Which loading dose of magnesium sulfate is recommended by NICE?
A.why: NG133 1.8.4 uses the Collaborative Eclampsia Trial regimen: a loading dose of 4 g IV over 5 to 15 minutes, followed by 1 g per hour for 24 hours.

whyNot.0: 2 g is not the loading dose and 30 minutes is slower than the regimen; 2 to 4 g is the extra dose for a recurrent fit.
whyNot.2: NICE recommends the intravenous regimen; the IM route is not the NG133 regimen.
whyNot.3: 1 g is the hourly maintenance dose, not the loading dose.

A.q: A woman receiving a magnesium sulfate infusion has no patellar reflex when the midwife checks. What does this finding most likely indicate?
A.why: The SPC states that disappearance of the deep tendon reflex is a useful clinical sign of the onset of magnesium intoxication, before respiratory depression.

whyNot.0: A tissued cannula would reduce the magnesium she receives, not abolish her reflexes.
whyNot.2: Worsening pre-eclampsia tends to cause brisk reflexes and clonus, not absent reflexes.
whyNot.3: Absent reflexes in a woman on magnesium must be treated as toxicity, not put down to a recent fit.

A.q: A woman with severe pre-eclampsia is on a magnesium sulfate infusion. What is the recommended limit for her maintenance fluids?
A.why: NG133 1.8.12 limits maintenance fluids in severe pre-eclampsia to 80 mL per hour unless there are ongoing fluid losses such as haemorrhage.

whyNot.0: 125 mL per hour is a typical general maintenance rate and risks pulmonary oedema in severe pre-eclampsia.
whyNot.1: 100 mL per hour exceeds the NG133 limit of 80 mL per hour.
whyNot.3: 60 mL per hour is not the NG133 figure; the limit is 80 mL per hour.

B.q: After an eclamptic fit, for how long should the magnesium sulfate maintenance infusion continue?
options: 24 hours after the birth of the baby
Until the blood pressure is under 140/90
B.why: NG133 1.8.4: continue 1 g per hour for 24 hours, and if she has had a fit, for 24 hours after the last fit.

whyNot.0: 12 hours is too short; the regimen runs for 24 hours.
whyNot.1: The clock runs from the last fit (or from starting, if no fit), not from the birth.
whyNot.2: Magnesium prevents fits; it is not titrated to blood pressure, which is treated with antihypertensives.

B.q: A woman with severe pre-eclampsia is ready for the birth. Which drug for active management of the third stage is most appropriate?
options: Oxytocin 5 units with ergometrine 500 micrograms IM
B.why: Oxytocin plus ergometrine is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia, eclampsia and severe hypertension (NG235 1.10.9), so oxytocin 10 units IM is used.

whyNot.1: Syntometrine contains ergometrine, which raises blood pressure and is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia.
whyNot.2: Ergometrine alone carries the same hypertensive risk and is contraindicated here.
whyNot.3: Carboprost is a treatment for PPH from uterine atony, not a routine third-stage prophylactic.

B.q: On a magnesium infusion, a woman's respiratory rate falls to 10 breaths per minute and she is drowsy. Which medicine should be immediately available?
B.why: Respiratory depression is a sign of magnesium toxicity; the SPC states calcium gluconate injection, the antidote, should be immediately available.

whyNot.2: Sodium bicarbonate does not antagonise magnesium.

C.q: Ama, 35 weeks, has BP 170/114, epigastric pain and blurred vision. The obstetrician plans IV hydralazine. Antenatally, what fluid does NICE advise before or with the first dose?
options: No fluid before the first dose
C.why: NG133 1.8.8: consider up to 500 mL crystalloid fluid before or at the same time as the first dose of IV hydralazine in the antenatal period.

whyNot.0: 1,000 mL is twice the recommended maximum and risks pulmonary oedema.
whyNot.1: NICE specifies crystalloid, not colloid, for this purpose.
whyNot.3: Hydralazine can cause a sharp fall in BP, so a small crystalloid volume is advised antenatally.

C.q: A woman on magnesium sulfate after an eclamptic fit has passed 40 mL of urine in the last 2 hours. Why is this important for her magnesium therapy?
options: It shows the fluid limit is too strict
It suggests the dose is too low
It means the infusion can stop
Magnesium may accumulate to toxic levels
C.why: Magnesium is excreted by the kidneys; the SPC warns urine output should not fall below 25 mL per hour, as hypermagnesaemia can follow. 20 mL per hour needs urgent medical review.

whyNot.0: Oliguria is a feature of severe pre-eclampsia; increasing fluids risks pulmonary oedema and does not address the toxicity risk.
whyNot.1: Poor urine output raises magnesium levels; it does not mean she is underdosed.
whyNot.2: Low urine output is a warning sign, not an end point for therapy.

C.q: A woman with eclampsia has a second fit 2 hours into her magnesium maintenance infusion. What further treatment does NICE recommend?
options: A further 2 to 4 g magnesium IV
C.why: NG133 1.8.4: for recurrent fits give a further dose of 2 to 4 g magnesium sulfate IV over 5 to 15 minutes.

whyNot.0: NG133 1.8.5: do not use diazepam as an alternative to magnesium sulfate in eclampsia.
whyNot.2: Phenytoin is also specifically not recommended as an alternative to magnesium sulfate.
whyNot.3: The regimen for a recurrent fit is a bolus of 2 to 4 g, not doubling the maintenance rate.

reteach.title: Magnesium as a seatbelt for the brain
reteach.question: Think of magnesium sulfate as a seatbelt: it protects against fits, but pulled too tight it stops breathing. How does the midwife keep it in the safe zone?

blocks.body: Magnesium sulfate is the drug that stops and prevents eclamptic fits. It is loaded fast (4 g over 5 to 15 minutes) and then dripped steadily (1 g an hour for 24 hours). Because the kidneys clear it, poor urine output lets it build up. The first sign of too much is the knee reflex disappearing; next comes slow breathing. So the midwife checks the reflex, the breathing and the urine, and has calcium gluconate ready.

blocks.h: Toxicity signs in order of severity (SPC 4.8-4.9)

blocks.text: Brisk reflexes and clonus point to worsening pre-eclampsia; absent reflexes in a woman on magnesium point to toxicity.

explain.body: Severe hypertension is a systolic over 160 or diastolic over 110 (NG133). Severe features include severe headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain, vomiting, oliguria with severe hypertension and worsening bloods. These should prompt urgent review and consideration of magnesium sulfate (1.8.3).

items.label: BP checks in labour when severe

test.q: A woman with pre-eclampsia at 35 weeks reports a severe headache and flashing lights. What does this indicate?
test.why: Severe headache and visual disturbance are severe features of pre-eclampsia (NG133 1.1.1, 1.8.3) needing urgent assessment.

whyNot.0: These are red-flag symptoms, not normal tiredness.
whyNot.1: In a woman with pre-eclampsia, headache with visual disturbance must be treated as disease progression first.
whyNot.3: Attributing new neurological symptoms to anxiety risks missing impending eclampsia.

explain.body: Loading dose 4 g IV over 5 to 15 minutes, then 1 g per hour for 24 hours, continued 24 hours after the last fit. A recurrent fit needs a further 2 to 4 g over 5 to 15 minutes (NG133 1.8.4).

test.q: What is the hourly maintenance dose of magnesium sulfate after the loading dose in the NICE regimen?
test.why: NG133 1.8.4: maintenance infusion of 1 g per hour for 24 hours.

whyNot.0: 0.5 g per hour is below the recommended maintenance dose.
whyNot.2: 2 g per hour is double the NG133 maintenance dose.
whyNot.3: 4 g is the loading dose, not an hourly rate.

explain.body: The SPC asks for checks of the patellar reflex, a respiratory rate of at least 16 per minute and urine output of at least 25 mL per hour. Loss of the deep tendon reflex is the early sign; respiratory paralysis is late. Calcium gluconate is the antidote and should be immediately available.

test.q: Which finding should a midwife regard as the earliest clinical sign of magnesium toxicity?
test.why: SPC 4.9: disappearance of the deep tendon reflex is a useful clinical sign of the onset of magnesium intoxication.

whyNot.1: Magnesium intoxication causes a fall in blood pressure, not a rise.
whyNot.2: Brisk reflexes and clonus are signs of worsening pre-eclampsia, not toxicity.
whyNot.3: Tachycardia is not the recognised early sign of magnesium toxicity.

explain.body: Treat severe hypertension with labetalol, oral nifedipine or IV hydralazine (NG133 1.8.6). Limit maintenance fluids to 80 mL per hour unless there are ongoing losses (1.8.12), and avoid volume expansion unless hydralazine is the antenatal antihypertensive (1.8.11). No routine preload before an epidural (1.7.6).

test.q: A woman with severe pre-eclampsia requests an epidural in labour. What does NICE advise about IV fluid preloading?
options: Do not preload with IV fluids
test.why: NG133 1.7.6: do not preload women who have severe pre-eclampsia with IV fluids before establishing low-dose epidural analgesia.

whyNot.0: A large preload risks pulmonary oedema in severe pre-eclampsia.
whyNot.1: Colloid preload is also volume expansion, which NICE advises against here.
whyNot.2: Routine fluid with each top-up is not recommended and risks fluid overload.
